kurzfassung: Gynecologist Dr. Joelle Osias discusses the limitations of traditional treatments for endometriosis, such as repeated surgeries and hormonal suppression, which often ignore the root causes of the disease. She advocates for a whole-body approach that includes gut health, personalized nutrition, and off-label peptide therapies like GLP-1s to reduce chronic inflammation. The conversation highlights the friction between rigid medical guidelines and personalized medicine, encouraging patients to take an active role in their healthcare.
stichpunkte: Endometriosis affects about one in ten women, taking seven to ten years on average to diagnose because painful periods are often normalized.
The disease is now recognized as a whole-body autoimmune and inflammatory condition rather than purely a reproductive one.
Traditional medical standards rely heavily on hormonal therapies and repeated laparoscopic surgeries, which fail to address underlying root causes.
Impaired immune cell function and gut health issues, such as increased intestinal permeability, contribute significantly to chronic inflammation.
Off-label treatments like GLP-1 receptor agonists and peptides such as BPC-157 help lower systemic inflammation and manage metabolic imbalances.
Corporate healthcare models and rigid medical guidelines create barriers for physicians attempting to provide personalized and holistic care.
Patient advocacy and education are critical for navigating complex health conditions and finding effective long-term solutions.

beschreibung:
Why do so many patients — not just those with endometriosis — end up cycling through specialists, labs, and prescriptions without ever getting a real answer? In this episode, Dr. Kylie Burton and Jessica Brickie sit down with gynecologist and women's health advocate Dr. Joelle Osias to make the case for a different model of medicine altogether: one built on root causes, individualized labs, and tools like peptides and GLP-1s that fall outside the standard playbook.
Dr. Osias uses her own path — from Stanford- and Johns Hopkins-trained gynecologist to outspoken advocate for personalized medicine — to explain why "standard of care" so often means algorithmic, one-size-fits-all treatment, and what changes when a physician is willing to look at the whole body instead of just their assigned specialty. She and the hosts trace that thinking through endometriosis as a case study (its whole-body, autoimmune nature, the limits of hormones and repeat surgery), but the conversation ranges well beyond it — into gut health and food sensitivities, thyroid testing gaps, vitamin D, peptides like BPC-157 and KPV, and the growing off-label use of GLP-1s for inflammation, PCOS, cardiovascular risk, and even cancer prevention. Jessica also shares her own diagnosis story from 1990, grounding the discussion in just how far — and how little — medicine has moved in three decades.
Whether or not endometriosis is part of your story, this episode is really about a bigger question: what does it look like to treat the whole patient, and what tools exist for that once you step outside the standard of care?

What You'll Learn
Why "standard of care" is often algorithmic by design — and what gets lost when medicine treats patients as a protocol instead of an individual
How Dr. Osias started incorporating peptides (including BPC-157 and KPV) into patient care, and the regulatory hurdles around off-label and non-FDA-indicated treatments
GLP-1 microdosing for inflammation, PCOS, cardiovascular risk, and more — including why standard pharmaceutical dosing doesn't fit every patient
The gut-immune connection, food sensitivities, and why 80% of the immune system lives in the gut
Commonly missed labs: free T3, reverse T3, vitamin D, ferritin — and why standard panels can miss real dysfunction
The challenges of accessing peptide and GLP-1 therapy for adolescent patients
Endometriosis as a case study: what it actually is, why it's better understood as a whole-body autoimmune-inflammatory condition, and why surgery and hormones alone so often fall short
The risks of early hysterectomy and why Dr. Osias considers it a last resort, not a first-line fix
Why Dr. Osias believes personalized medicine, not algorithmic standard-of-care protocols, is the future of healthcare — for women and men alike

Guest
Dr. Joelle Osias is a gynecologist, entrepreneur, and women's health advocate based in Menlo Park, California. She trained at Tufts University and Stanford University School of Medicine, completed her residency at Johns Hopkins, and pursued advanced training through the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and Stanford Graduate School of Business. Her practice focuses on endometriosis, menopausal care, weight management, and personalized, longevity-focused medicine.
